scope: MEAS: Internet Archive metadata and file listing for BERGViolinConcerto-NEWTRANSFER, MD5 of the cached MP3 against the manifest, loudness and spectral-centroid traces, tuning estimate, spectral-peak and pitch tracking of the opening and of the row entry; EXT: The American Music Lover, September 1941 (OCR of the Internet Archive scan), Columbia Record Catalog 1942 (OCR), Steinberg’s note on bso.org, Douglas Jarman in Musicologica Austriaca (2017, CC BY 4.0), IMSLP work page, Wikipedia, the Discogs listing of the 2023 Sony box set, the Bach Cantatas Website discography. Not an aural review.

corrections.finding: The row cue and section B stood at 75 s. The solo violin begins the rising row on the open G at about 66.3 s (G3 near 199 Hz), then B♭3, D4, F♯4, A4 and C5 between 67 and 70 s, and reaches F6 at 74–75 s, so 75 s is where the first ascent ends. Jarman puts the row and its inversion on the solo violin at bars 15–27. A pause of 0.6 s at 64.0–64.6 s precedes the accompanying figure.
corrections.fix: Section B moved to 65 s and the cue to 66 s (basis audio-feature); Jarman added to the evidence.

corrections.finding: The life note about Krasner at the Wörthersee (60 s) sat six seconds before the row cue.
corrections.fix: Moved to 30 s, in the quiet prelude.

corrections.finding: “Krasner stayed with Berg” goes beyond Steinberg, who writes that Krasner was able to spend some time with Berg at the country house.
corrections.fix: Text now says Krasner spent some time with Berg.

corrections.finding: The dossier gave the session date from the uploader’s description only and said the place was unknown; it described MM 465 as a “manual-sequence form”, which no consulted source says; and it dated public-domain status in Canada to 2006 together with the EU.
corrections.fix: Date now also rests on the Sony box-set listing (Discogs) and the Bach Cantatas discography, which both give 15 December 1940 and Severance Hall, Cleveland; the place is recorded as documented; the label field no longer interprets the prefix; the composition field separates the EU from Canada (IMSLP marks Canada and life-plus-50 countries as public domain).

checks.source: The Archive lists 01.I.AndanteAllegretto.mp3 as the uploaded VBR MP3, 631.04 s; the cached copy has the manifest MD5 (8ac16513…). The file opens with about 5 s of near-silence and ends with 5.4 s of silence after the last sound at about 625.6 s. The licence field reads CC BY-NC-SA 3.0.
checks.durationAndPitch: Movement I runs 10:31 and movement II 12:19, 22:50 in all; the Bach Cantatas discography gives 22:52 for the Naxos 9.80226 CD of this recording, so the transfer runs at the speed of a commercial reissue. Tuning estimate +26 cents for this file (90 s windows between +10 and +31 cents). The soloist’s open strings in the prelude measure G3 199 Hz, D4 299 Hz, A4 449.5 Hz, E5 670 Hz, that is +28 to +37 cents; the global key estimate is G minor, matching the row’s G. No error of a semitone or more; no correction applied.
checks.identity: Archive description: Krasner, Cleveland Orchestra, Rodzinski, Columbia set MM 465, matrices XCO 29764–29769, recorded 15 December 1940, “First Recording”, transfer by F. Reeder. American Music Lover, Sept. 1941: “Columbia set M-465, three discs, price $3.50”, Krasner, Cleveland Orchestra, Rodzinski. Columbia Record Catalog 1942: “6 sides, set M-465 … Krasner … Rodzinski cond. (11589-D—11591-D)”. Discogs listing of the Sony box set: “Cleveland, Severance Hall, December 15, 1940”. The Bach Cantatas page heads the entry “recorded live”; the issue is the commercial six-side Columbia set and the file begins and ends in silence with no applause.
checks.notes: Every cue was checked against Steinberg’s note on bso.org (opening, Wörthersee visit and 16 July letter, the row, the Manon Gropius programme, wienerisch/rustico, the folk song) and against the 1941 review (“musicianship and taste are strikingly displayed”, “clarity of line and detail”). Times: the Allegretto at 262 s follows a near-silence of 1.3 s (261.0–262.3 s) at the end of the Andante; the row entry was corrected as above; the review note at 330 s and the folk-song note at 490 s are world notes and carry no instant claim. Counts: 7 notes, limit 16. Voice rules read by hand and by the validator; validate.mjs prints ok for the listen file and the dossier.
checks.sideJoins: Near-silent gaps occur at 261.0–262.3 s and, shorter, near 417–419 s and 439–447 s. The set’s side boundaries are not documented, so none is asserted; the only cue at a gap is the Allegretto at 262 s, which is the end of the Andante.

rights.decision: Publish on the territorial basis stated in the file; the uploader’s licence label is not relied on.
rights.reasoning: (1) First publication: Columbia set M-465 was reviewed in The American Music Lover, vol. 8 no. 1, September 1941, pp. 17–18 (masthead “September 1941”, review signed P.H.R.), and listed in the Columbia Record Catalog of 1942. A recording first published in 1941 had no 50-year EU term left after 1991, before the 2011 extension, which reached only recordings still protected in 2013. (2) Provenance: a commercial studio-style session issue, not a live or broadcast capture; the Bach Cantatas page’s “recorded live” is not borne out by the six-side set. (3) The Archive item carries CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, applied in 2013 by the collector who made the transfer. The dossier credits him and does not rely on the label; the earlier candidate list excluded this transfer for the NC term, and tools/validate.mjs accepts any “CC BY…” label, so the validator does not test it. The site should keep the credit line. (4) The United States status of a 1940 recording is not established and the dossier says so. (5) Composition: Berg died in 1935; public domain in the EU since 2006, probably still protected in the United States (IMSLP); stated separately in the dossier.
rights.internetArchiveFlags: Metadata has no dark, access-restricted, noindex or litigation flag; collections are 78rpm and audio_music; no reviews.

observations.finding: The folk-song note stands at 490 s. I could not locate the tune in the audio; the most diatonic stretch of the Allegretto lies around 430–466 s, where the texture is sparse and divided by short pauses. The note is a world note and says only that the tune is passed among horn, violin and trumpets in this movement.
observations.action: Left unchanged; a score-aligned time would settle it.
